slides.question: How does relational data modeling eliminate redundancy through Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF)?

points: **Relational Modeling** splits information across separate logical tables to eliminate anomalies and redundancy.
**1NF (First Normal Form)**: Each cell contains a single atomic value; no repeating groups or comma-separated lists.
**2NF (Second Normal Form)**: Table is in 1NF and all non-key columns depend on the entire candidate key.
**3NF (Third Normal Form)**: Table is in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies (no non-key column depends on another non-key column).
Instead of duplicating author names inside every book row, we link `books.author_id` to `authors.id`.
explanation.highlight: Normalization separates entities into distinct tables, eliminating data redundancy and update anomalies.

slides.code:
-- Inspect relational separation between books and authors
SELECT 
  b.id AS book_id,
  b.title,
  b.author_id,
  a.name AS author_name,
  a.country
FROM books b
JOIN authors a ON b.author_id = a.id
LIMIT 5;
slides.tip: Show what happens when an author changes their name: in normalized design, you update exactly 1 row in authors.

slides.question: How are 1-to-1, 1-to-Many, and Many-to-Many relationships modeled in relational databases?

points: **1-to-1 (1:1)**: E.g., User and UserProfile. Primary key of child is also foreign key to parent.
**1-to-Many (1:N)**: E.g., One Customer has many Orders. Foreign key `customer_id` lives on the `orders` table.
**Many-to-Many (N:M)**: E.g., Orders and Books. Modeled using an intermediate **Junction Table** (`order_items`).
The junction table holds foreign keys to both parent tables plus line-item specific data (e.g., `quantity`, `unit_price`).
explanation.highlight: Model Many-to-Many relationships with a junction table linking two One-to-Many relationships.

slides.code:
-- Inspect the junction table order_items linking orders to books
SELECT 
  oi.order_id,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  b.title AS purchased_book,
  oi.quantity,
  oi.unit_price
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN books b ON oi.book_id = b.id
LIMIT 5;
slides.tip: Have learners trace how an order can have multiple books, and a book can appear in multiple orders via order_items.

data.note: Resolves N:M relationship between Orders and Books

slides.question: How do INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER JOINs match records across tables?

points: **`INNER JOIN`**: Returns only rows where there is a match in **BOTH** tables.
**`LEFT JOIN` (or LEFT OUTER JOIN)**: Returns **ALL** rows from the left table, with matching right table rows or `NULL` if no match exists.
**`RIGHT JOIN`**: Returns **ALL** rows from the right table, matching left or `NULL`.
**`FULL OUTER JOIN`**: Returns all rows when there is a match in either table (combines LEFT and RIGHT).
Use table aliases (`FROM books b JOIN authors a`) to keep queries concise.
explanation.highlight: INNER JOIN keeps only matches; LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows and fills unmatched rights with NULL.

slides.code:
-- Compare INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN
-- 1. INNER JOIN: Only customers with orders
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total_amount
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;

-- 2. LEFT JOIN: All customers including those who never purchased
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total_amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id;
slides.tip: Show the visual Venn diagram in the left panel to clearly see row preservation.

slides.question: How does a SELF JOIN query hierarchical data within the same table?

points: A **`SELF JOIN`** joins a table to itself by using two distinct table aliases (e.g. `FROM employees e JOIN employees m`).
Standard use case: **Hierarchies & Org Charts** where a row's `manager_id` points back to another row's `id` in the same table.
Another use case: Finding pairs or duplicates (e.g., books with the exact same price).
Always use `LEFT JOIN` for self-joins on hierarchies so the top-level CEO/root (whose `manager_id IS NULL`) is not filtered out.
explanation.highlight: Join a table to itself using two distinct aliases to navigate hierarchies and manager relationships.

slides.code:
-- Self-Join: List employees alongside their managers
SELECT 
  e.name AS employee_name,
  e.department,
  COALESCE(m.name, 'Top Executive / CEO') AS manager_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY e.department, e.name;
slides.tip: Demonstrate why LEFT JOIN is necessary: without it, Sarah Connor (the CEO) disappears from the output.

slides.question: Module 5 Quiz: Test your grasp of relational JOINs and normalization

points: Verify your ability to select the correct JOIN type for real business requirements.
Test your understanding of NULL handling in unmatched LEFT JOIN records.
Answer the 4 questions in the interactive quiz card.
explanation.highlight: Score 4/4 to demonstrate complete mastery of relational JOIN logic.

slides.tip: Review Cartesian products (CROSS JOIN) caused by omitted ON clauses.

questions.question: Which JOIN returns all records from the left table even if there is no match in the right table?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN guarantees that all rows from the left table are returned, filling unmatched columns with NULL.

questions.question: What happens if you omit the 'ON' clause in a JOIN statement?
options: The database throws a syntax error or performs a CROSS JOIN (Cartesian product)
It automatically matches columns with the same name
It only joins the first row
It creates a new table automatically
questions.explanation: Omitting the join condition produces a Cartesian product where every left row pairs with every right row (N x M rows).

questions.question: In an organization hierarchy where employees have a manager_id, what type of query connects them?
options: Self JOIN (joining the employees table to itself)
questions.explanation: A self-join with two aliases (e.g. 'employees e' and 'employees m') navigates parent-child relationships within one table.

questions.question: Which set operator combines results from two queries and removes duplicate rows?
questions.explanation: UNION combines result sets and performs deduplication. UNION ALL keeps all duplicate rows and is faster.

slides.question: How do FOREIGN KEY constraints preserve Referential Integrity across tables?

points: A **`FOREIGN KEY`** matches the `PRIMARY KEY` of another table, ensuring a child record cannot reference a non-existent parent.
Referential actions on delete/update:
- **`ON DELETE CASCADE`**: Deleting the parent automatically deletes all its children.
- **`ON DELETE SET NULL`**: Sets the child foreign key column to NULL when the parent is deleted.
- **`ON DELETE RESTRICT` (Default)**: Rejects parent deletion if child rows still reference it.
In SQLite, execute `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` to enforce foreign key checking.
explanation.highlight: Foreign keys prevent orphan records and maintain strict referential integrity across related tables.

slides.tip: Point out how ON DELETE CASCADE is great for line items in orders, but dangerous for users with financial records.

slides.question: How do UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT combine multiple query result sets?

points: Set operators combine the outputs of two or more independent `SELECT` statements.
**Requirements**: Both queries must return the **same number of columns** with compatible data types.
**`UNION`**: Combines datasets and **removes duplicates** (requires a sort/hash step).
**`UNION ALL`**: Combines datasets and **keeps all duplicates** (very fast, zero sorting overhead).
**`INTERSECT`**: Returns only rows present in **BOTH** queries.
**`EXCEPT` (or MINUS)**: Returns rows present in the first query but **NOT** in the second.
explanation.highlight: Use UNION ALL when duplicate removal is unnecessary for significantly faster query performance.

slides.code:
-- 1. UNION: Unique list of all countries across authors and customers
SELECT country FROM authors
UNION
SELECT country FROM customers;

-- 2. INTERSECT: Countries that have BOTH authors AND customers
SELECT country FROM authors
INTERSECT
SELECT country FROM customers;
slides.tip: Demonstrate how UNION ALL runs in O(N+M) while UNION requires an O((N+M) log (N+M)) deduplication sort.

data.note: Countries appearing in both authors and customers

slides.question: How do SQL Views encapsulate complex multi-table joins as reusable virtual tables?

points: A **`VIEW`** is a stored, named query definition that behaves like a virtual table: `CREATE VIEW view_name AS SELECT ...;`.
Views do **not** store physical data on disk (unless materialized); they re-execute the underlying query when queried.
Benefits: Encapsulates complex joins, simplifies frontend reporting, and restricts access to sensitive columns (e.g. hiding employee salaries).
Querying a view is as simple as `SELECT * FROM view_name WHERE ...`.
explanation.highlight: Views encapsulate multi-table join complexity behind a simple virtual table interface.

slides.code:
-- Create a reusable view for order fulfillment
CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS v_order_summary AS
SELECT 
  o.id AS order_id,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  c.email,
  o.order_date,
  o.total_amount,
  o.status
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;

-- Query the virtual view
SELECT * FROM v_order_summary WHERE status = 'COMPLETED';
slides.tip: Explain the security advantage: you can grant analysts access to a view without exposing underlying tables.

data.note: Virtual table dynamically computed upon execution

slides.question: Challenge: Identify churned or inactive customers who have never made a purchase

points: **Task**: Find all registered customers who have **NEVER** placed an order.
**Approach**: Use a `LEFT JOIN` between `customers` and `orders`, and filter where `orders.id IS NULL`.
Return `customers.id`, `name`, `email`, and `country`.
explanation.highlight: Execute LEFT JOIN orders ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL to find non-purchasers.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR QUERY HERE:
SELECT c.id, c.name, c.email, c.country
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.name ASC;
slides.tip: This 'anti-join' pattern with LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL is an essential SQL interview classic.

solution.approach: Perform a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders. Unmatched customers will receive NULL for all order columns. Filter with WHERE o.id IS NULL.
solution.code:
SELECT c.id, c.name, c.email, c.country
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.name ASC;
explanationPoints: LEFT JOIN retains every customer regardless of whether orders exist.
Customers with zero orders have `NULL` in the order fields.
`WHERE o.id IS NULL` isolates these non-purchasing customers.

slides.question: Challenge: Fetch customer names for the 3 most recent transactions

points: **Task**: Retrieve the 3 most recent orders in the system.
**Details**: Return `orders.id AS order_id`, `customers.name AS customer_name`, `orders.order_date`, and `orders.total_amount`.
**Ordering**: Sort by `orders.order_date` DESC, `orders.id` DESC.
**Limit**: Return exactly 3 rows.
explanation.highlight: Join orders with customers, sort by order_date DESC, and limit to 3 records.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR QUERY HERE:
SELECT 
  o.id AS order_id,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  o.order_date,
  o.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.id DESC
LIMIT 3;
slides.tip: Demonstrate how an index on (order_date DESC) allows this query to return instantly without scanning the whole orders table.

solution.approach: INNER JOIN orders and customers on customer_id = id, sort by order_date DESC, and cap with LIMIT 3.
solution.code:
SELECT 
  o.id AS order_id,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  o.order_date,
  o.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.id DESC
LIMIT 3;
solution.timeComplexity: O(N log K) with top-K index
explanationPoints: INNER JOIN connects order transactions to their corresponding customer accounts.
`ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.id DESC` sorts newest orders first with an ID tiebreaker.
`LIMIT 3` ensures only the top 3 recent orders are delivered.

slides.question: Challenge: Filter high-ticket purchases exceeding $50.00

points: **Task**: Find all orders where `total_amount >= 50.00`.
Return `order_id`, `customer_name`, `email`, and `total_amount`.
Sort by `total_amount` DESC.
explanation.highlight: INNER JOIN customers with orders filtering WHERE total_amount >= 50.00.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR QUERY HERE:
SELECT 
  o.id AS order_id,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  c.email,
  o.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total_amount >= 50.00
ORDER BY o.total_amount DESC;
slides.tip: Show students how sales teams use this exact query to trigger VIP concierge thank-you emails.

solution.approach: Join orders and customers, filter with WHERE total_amount >= 50.00, and sort DESC.
solution.code:
SELECT 
  o.id AS order_id,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  c.email,
  o.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total_amount >= 50.00
ORDER BY o.total_amount DESC;
explanationPoints: The WHERE condition filters out smaller retail orders.
Joining on `customer_id` extracts customer email contact info.

slides.question: Challenge: Identify all buyers of 'Clean Code'

points: **Task**: Find the names and emails of all customers who purchased the book titled `'Clean Code'`.
**Tables needed**: `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, and `books` (a 4-table join!).
Use `DISTINCT` on customer name to avoid listing the same customer twice if they bought it multiple times.
explanation.highlight: Perform a 4-table relational join from customers to books via orders and order_items.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR 4-TABLE JOIN HERE:
SELECT DISTINCT 
  c.name AS customer_name,
  c.email
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
JOIN books b ON oi.book_id = b.id
WHERE b.title = 'Clean Code'
ORDER BY c.name ASC;
slides.tip: This challenge demonstrates the power of relational algebra: traversing from User -> Order -> Item -> Product.

solution.approach: Traverse the relationship path: customers -> orders -> order_items -> books with WHERE b.title = 'Clean Code'.
solution.code:
SELECT DISTINCT 
  c.name AS customer_name,
  c.email
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
JOIN books b ON oi.book_id = b.id
WHERE b.title = 'Clean Code'
ORDER BY c.name ASC;
explanationPoints: We chain 3 JOINs together following primary/foreign key connections.
`WHERE b.title = 'Clean Code'` filters the line item graph.
`DISTINCT` prevents multiple rows if a customer bought Clean Code across multiple orders.

slides.question: Challenge: Build a referral marketing report using a Self-Join

points: **Task**: Write a `SELF JOIN` on the `customers` table to display who referred whom.
Return:
- `referred_customer`: The new customer's name (`c.name`)
- `referrer_name`: The referring customer's name (`r.name`)
- `country`: The referred customer's country
Only include customers who were referred (`WHERE c.referrer_id IS NOT NULL`).
explanation.highlight: Join customers c with customers r ON c.referrer_id = r.id to pair new users with referrers.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR SELF JOIN HERE:
SELECT 
  c.name AS referred_customer,
  r.name AS referrer_name,
  c.country
FROM customers c
JOIN customers r ON c.referrer_id = r.id
ORDER BY referrer_name, referred_customer;
slides.tip: Demonstrate how referral networks and invite rewards depend on self-referential foreign keys.

solution.approach: Self-join customers as 'c' (the referee) and customers as 'r' (the referrer) on c.referrer_id = r.id.
solution.code:
SELECT 
  c.name AS referred_customer,
  r.name AS referrer_name,
  c.country
FROM customers c
JOIN customers r ON c.referrer_id = r.id
ORDER BY referrer_name, referred_customer;
explanationPoints: `customers c` represents the person who was referred.
`customers r` represents the existing member who shared their referral link.
`c.referrer_id = r.id` matches the relationship correctly.

slides.question: Challenge: Co-purchase book recommendation engine

points: **Task**: Find pairs of distinct books that were purchased together in the **same order**.
Join `order_items oi1` with `order_items oi2` ON `oi1.order_id = oi2.order_id` AND `oi1.book_id < oi2.book_id`.
Join with `books` to get the titles.
Return `b1.title AS book_1` and `b2.title AS book_2`.
explanation.highlight: Self-join order_items with oi1.book_id < oi2.book_id to find items bought in the same order.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR CO-PURCHASE QUERY HERE:
SELECT DISTINCT 
  b1.title AS book_1,
  b2.title AS book_2
FROM order_items oi1
JOIN order_items oi2 ON oi1.order_id = oi2.order_id AND oi1.book_id < oi2.book_id
JOIN books b1 ON oi1.book_id = b1.id
JOIN books b2 ON oi2.book_id = b2.id
ORDER BY book_1, book_2;
slides.tip: Explain why the '<' comparison is crucial: it prevents pairing a book with itself and avoids mirror duplicates (A, B and B, A).

solution.approach: Join order_items to itself matching on order_id with book_id inequality, then join book titles.
solution.code:
SELECT DISTINCT 
  b1.title AS book_1,
  b2.title AS book_2
FROM order_items oi1
JOIN order_items oi2 ON oi1.order_id = oi2.order_id AND oi1.book_id < oi2.book_id
JOIN books b1 ON oi1.book_id = b1.id
JOIN books b2 ON oi2.book_id = b2.id
ORDER BY book_1, book_2;
explanationPoints: `oi1.order_id = oi2.order_id` ensures both items were purchased in the same shopping cart.
`oi1.book_id < oi2.book_id` strictly prevents a book matching itself and eliminates reverse duplicate pairs.
This is the foundational SQL pattern behind 'Customers who bought this also bought' recommendations.

slides.question: Challenge: Find pairs of distinct books that share the exact same price

points: **Task**: Use a self-join on `books` to find distinct pairs of books that have identical prices (`price`).
Use `b1.id < b2.id` to avoid self-matches and reverse duplicates.
Return `b1.title AS book_1`, `b2.title AS book_2`, and `b1.price AS shared_price`.
Order by `shared_price` DESC.
explanation.highlight: Join books b1 with books b2 ON b1.price = b2.price AND b1.id < b2.id.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR QUERY HERE:
SELECT 
  b1.title AS book_1,
  b2.title AS book_2,
  b1.price AS shared_price
FROM books b1
JOIN books b2 ON b1.price = b2.price AND b1.id < b2.id
ORDER BY shared_price DESC;
slides.tip: Point out how id < id is the universal SQL trick for pairwise non-duplicate combinations.

solution.approach: Join books b1 with books b2 on price equality and id inequality.
solution.code:
SELECT 
  b1.title AS book_1,
  b2.title AS book_2,
  b1.price AS shared_price
FROM books b1
JOIN books b2 ON b1.price = b2.price AND b1.id < b2.id
ORDER BY shared_price DESC;
solution.timeComplexity: O(N log N) with price index
explanationPoints: `b1.price = b2.price` matches books with identical price tags.
`b1.id < b2.id` ensures each pair is generated exactly once.

slides.question: Challenge: Find authors whose catalog spans multiple technical categories

points: **Task**: Find authors who have written books in at least two distinct categories.
Self-join `books b1` and `books b2` on `b1.author_id = b2.author_id AND b1.category != b2.category`.
Join with `authors` to retrieve the author's name.
Use `DISTINCT` to return unique author names.
explanation.highlight: Join books b1 with books b2 on author_id with distinct categories to find versatile writers.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR QUERY HERE:
SELECT DISTINCT 
  a.name AS author_name
FROM books b1
JOIN books b2 ON b1.author_id = b2.author_id AND b1.category != b2.category
JOIN authors a ON b1.author_id = a.id
ORDER BY author_name ASC;
slides.tip: This pattern queries domain diversity across relational entities without requiring GROUP BY.

solution.approach: Self-join books on author_id where category != category, then resolve author names via authors table.
solution.code:
SELECT DISTINCT 
  a.name AS author_name
FROM books b1
JOIN books b2 ON b1.author_id = b2.author_id AND b1.category != b2.category
JOIN authors a ON b1.author_id = a.id
ORDER BY author_name ASC;
explanationPoints: `b1.category != b2.category` checks that an author has at least two different category classifications.
Joining on `authors` surfaces human-readable author names.

slides.question: Challenge: Join books with author tiers and publisher revenue

points: **Task**: List all books with `price >= 40.00` along with their author's name and country.
Return `b.title`, `b.price`, `a.name AS author_name`, and `a.country`.
Sort by `b.price` DESC.
explanation.highlight: Perform an INNER JOIN between books and authors filtering on price >= 40.00.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR QUERY HERE:
SELECT 
  b.title,
  b.price,
  a.name AS author_name,
  a.country
FROM books b
JOIN authors a ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE b.price >= 40.00
ORDER BY b.price DESC;
slides.tip: Show how standard 2-table joins power product detail pages in production.

solution.approach: Join books with authors on author_id = id and filter on price >= 40.00.
solution.code:
SELECT 
  b.title,
  b.price,
  a.name AS author_name,
  a.country
FROM books b
JOIN authors a ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE b.price >= 40.00
ORDER BY b.price DESC;
explanationPoints: Matches book rows to their author biography details.
Filters the result set to premium technical literature.

slides.question: Challenge: Identify books that have appeared in multiple order line items

points: **Task**: Find the titles of all books that have been ordered in at least one transaction.
Join `books` with `order_items` on `books.id = order_items.book_id`.
Use `DISTINCT` on `books.title`.
Sort alphabetically.
explanation.highlight: Join books with order_items using DISTINCT to list all actively ordered inventory items.

slides.code:
-- WRITE YOUR QUERY HERE:
SELECT DISTINCT 
  b.id AS book_id,
  b.title,
  b.price
FROM books b
JOIN order_items oi ON b.id = oi.book_id
ORDER BY b.title ASC;
slides.tip: Contrast this with the inactive customer query to demonstrate operational catalog metrics.

solution.approach: INNER JOIN books and order_items on book_id = id and project distinct book records.
solution.code:
SELECT DISTINCT 
  b.id AS book_id,
  b.title,
  b.price
FROM books b
JOIN order_items oi ON b.id = oi.book_id
ORDER BY b.title ASC;
explanationPoints: INNER JOIN naturally filters out any book that has never been ordered.
`DISTINCT` ensures each book is listed only once regardless of total sales volume.
